For any affine algebraic set $X\subseteq k^n$, its coordinate ring is $$k[X]=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I(X).$$ Write $\bar x_i$ for the coordinate classes. The structure map sends $c\in k$ to its constant class; all $k$-algebras and maps are unital, with the zero algebra allowed. Thus $k[\varnothing]=0$, where $0=1$. Since $I(X)$ is radical by [[def-classical-vanishing-ideal]], $k[X]$ is reduced: $\bar f^{\,m}=0$ implies $f^m\in I(X)$ and hence $f\in I(X)$, so $\bar f=0$. A **classical algebraic prevariety** over k is a quasi-compact locally ringed space with a structure sheaf of k-algebras, covered by open subspaces isomorphic over k to these affine models. Here quasi-compact means every open cover has a finite subcover. Equivalently it admits a finite affine-model cover. To justify the converse, each affine model is quasi-compact: polynomial principal opens $D_Z(h)=\{z:h(z)\ne0\}$ form a basis. Given an open cover, take all h whose principal opens lie in a member. the quotient ideals and the closed subscheme unchanged. Thus $Z(s)$ depends
only on the parameter $[s]\in\mathbf P(W)$. The **base locus** of $W$ is the
closed subset
$$
\operatorname{Bs}(W)=\bigcap_{0\ne s\in W}|Z(s)|=\bigcap_{[s]\in\mathbf P(W)}|Z(s)|\subseteq X.
$$
It is closed because each $|Z(s)|$ is closed and arbitrary intersections of
closed subsets are closed.
It is **base-point-free** when this subset is empty.

Let $X$ be a scheme, let $L$ be an invertible (locally free of rank one)
$\mathcal O_X$-module, and let $s\in\Gamma(X,L)$. Choose an affine open cover
$U_i=\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ on which $L$ has a generator $e_i$, and write
$s|_{U_i}=f_i e_i$. The affine schemes
$\operatorname{Spec}(A_i/(f_i))$ glue, with their quotient maps, to a closed
subscheme $Z(s)\hookrightarrow X$ that is canonical up to unique isomorphism
over $X$ and independent of the chosen trivializations. The construction uses
the ideal $(f_i)$ itself, with no nonzerodivisor or reducedness hypothesis;
it retains nilpotents and includes the empty and whole zero schemes.

For every $n\in\mathbb Z$, let $\mathcal O(n)$ be the sheaf of
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1_k}$-modules glued from the structure sheaves
$\mathcal O_{U_0}$ and $\mathcal O_{U_\infty}$ with frames $e_0=1$ on $U_0$ and
$e_\infty=1$ on $U_\infty$, related on $W$ by
$$e_\infty=t^ne_0,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad e_0=t^{-n}e_\infty,$$
through the transition isomorphism given by multiplication by the unit $t^{-n}$
of $k[t,t^{-1}]$ ([[thm-gluing-sheaves]], [[def-gluing-datum-sheaves]]). Each
$\mathcal O(n)$ is an invertible sheaf: it is free of rank one on each chart with
the displayed frame. In particular $\mathcal O(0)$ is the structure sheaf
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1_k}$, and on the overlap the sections are written
$k[t,t^{-1}]e_0$, so that $a(t)e_0=t^{-n}a(t)e_\infty=u^na(u^{-1})e_\infty$.
A field $F$ is **algebraically closed** when every nonconstant polynomial $p\in F[x]$ has a root in $F$: there is $\lambda\in F$ such that $p(\lambda)=0$.

If $p$ is prime and $0<k<p$, then

Let $X$ be a scheme and $x\in X$. Write $C_xX=\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2$
for the intrinsic cotangent space from
[[def-zariski-cotangent-space-point]]. The **intrinsic Zariski tangent space**
of $X$ at $x$ is its linear dual over the residue field:
$$T_xX:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\kappa(x)}(C_xX,\kappa(x)).$$
If $\mathfrak m_x=0$, then $C_xX=0$ and $T_xX=0$.

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of
$k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put
$$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$
Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let
$f_1,\ldots,f_r$ be any finite generating list of the actual ideal $I$.
Then the coordinate-velocity map gives a canonical $k$-linear isomorphism
$$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$
The kernel is independent of the chosen finite generating list of $I$. No
reducedness, perfectness, or characteristic hypothesis is needed. Finiteness of
the list is available for every finite $n$ by the finite-variable polynomial
Noetherian result cited below.

Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian scheme and $x\in X$. Write
$R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, let $\mathfrak m_x$ be its maximal ideal, and set
$\kappa(x)=R/\mathfrak m_x$. The point $x$ is **regular** when $R$ is a
regular local ring, with regularity defined by
$\operatorname{edim}R=\dim R$. Then the intrinsic tangent space $T_xX$ is
finite-dimensional over $\kappa(x)$, and
$$x\text{ is regular}\Longleftrightarrow\dim_{\kappa(x)}T_xX=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}.$$
This is absolute regularity of the local ring; it asserts no smoothness over a
base field.
The **Krull dimension** of $R$ is the supremum of all integers $n\ge 0$ for which such a chain exists. This supremum is allowed to be infinite.

Let $k$ be a field and let $A$ be a commutative $k$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) whose underlying $k$-vector space is
finite dimensional, say $\dim_kA=n$ with $n\in\mathbb N$ ([[def-dimension]]).
Then $A$ is a Noetherian ring, and every ideal of $A$ is generated by at most
$n$ elements.

A scheme is **locally Noetherian** if it has an affine open cover by spectra of
Noetherian rings. It is **Noetherian** if it is locally Noetherian and
quasi-compact; equivalently, it has a finite affine open cover by spectra of
Noetherian rings.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field and
$X$ a finite-type $k$-scheme. Smoothness of $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is
defined by local standard smooth presentations in
[[def-smooth-morphism-classical]]. The following is an equivalent
characterization: $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth if and only if, for
every field extension $K/k$, every local ring of the scheme-theoretic base
change $X_K$ is regular. Here $X_K$ is formed by tensoring affine coordinate
rings with $K$ and gluing as in
[[thm-ag-field-extension-of-schemes]]. We call this condition geometric
regularity of $X$ over $k$. It retains nilpotents in every field change.

Being locally of finite type is affine-local on both source and target. A
quasi-compact morphism locally of finite type is of finite type; equivalently,
over each affine target open it may be tested on a finite affine source cover.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.
The characteristic of a field is either $0$ or a prime number.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

derivations.claim: Compatibility on the overlap makes (1,u^p) and (t^p,1) global sections of O(p), and their restrictions to U_0 are k-linearly independent, so W=span{X^p,Y^p} is a 2-dimensional linear system.
k is perfect in the only sense used: every c in k is a p-th power, since z^p-c has a root; and p>=2.
Every parameter satisfies aX^p+bY^p=(alpha X+beta Y)^p with (alpha,beta) nonzero, so every member is the p-th power of a nonzero linear form.
On the two charts the member is Spec k[t]/(a+bt^p) and Spec k[u]/(au^p+b), computed with the unimposed local equation.
Every member is a single point with one chart equal to Spec k[tau]/(tau^p), so it has multiplicity p and no second point.
The system is base-point-free: the two coordinate sections are supported at the distinct points [0:1] and [1:0].
The local ring k[tau]/(tau^p) has Krull dimension 0 and is a finite-dimensional k-algebra, hence Noetherian and nonzero of k-dimension p.
The Jacobian of tau^p vanishes in characteristic p, so the tangent space at the point is 1-dimensional.
The member is locally Noetherian and at its point 1=dim T =/= 0 = dim O, so the point is not regular.
Each member is finite type over k and not smooth over k, by the contrapositive of the geometric-regularity criterion at K=k.

All parameters give non-smooth members while the parameter space is nonempty and the system is base-point-free, so the general member is not smooth and the arbitrary-system Bertini statement fails in characteristic p.

boundaries.evidence: Step 4.1 proves Bs(W)=empty, and step 3.1 shows a chart of a member can be empty without adding a second point; so the empty base locus and the empty-chart case are both handled.
Step 4.2 proves dim k[tau]/(tau^p)=0 with tau nilpotent and tau^p=0, so the zero-dimensional case is exactly the nonregular case; p>=2 by step 1.2 rules out tau=0.
Step 3.1 shows each member is cut by one equation and is a single point of multiplicity p with p>=2 from step 1.2, so the multiplicity-one case is excluded and cannot be confused with smoothness.
Step 2.2 uses the ideal generated by the local equation itself with no reduction, so the nonreduced ring k[tau]/(tau^p) of step 3.1 retains its nilpotents; nothing is reduced.

Step 1.1 uses L=O(p) with p>=2, the endpoint contrasting with the hyperplane case L=O(1) that is untouched; step 4.1 handles the two extreme parameters [1:0] and [0:1] giving the distinct points [0:1] and [1:0].
The only use of AC is step 7.1 through F13 (def-smooth-morphism-to-field-classical); the explicit witness uses the single extension K=k, so no selection from a family is made anywhere else.
Step 7.1 applies the forward implication smooth => geometric regularity in contrapositive form to Z(s) itself (K=k), so the used direction is fully accounted for.

boundaries.reason: The refutation only uses the direction smooth => all base-change local rings regular; the converse (regularity of base changes => smooth) is never invoked in any step of the counterexample.

risk_review.notes: The pencil spanned by X^p,Y^p on P¹ has no base point, but every nonzero member is (αX+βY)^p. Each zero scheme is a length-p fat point with local ring k[τ]/τ^p and is nonsmooth; this refutes the stated characteristic-p generalization, with p≥2.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field and
$f:X\to Y$ a morphism of finite-type $k$-schemes. The morphism $f$ is
**smooth** if every point $x\in X$ has affine neighborhoods
$x\in V=\operatorname{Spec}B$ and $f(x)\in U=\operatorname{Spec}A$, with
$f(V)\subseteq U$, for which the induced map $A\to B$ is standard smooth at
the prime corresponding to $x$ ([[def-ag-standard-smooth-algebra]]). Thus the
condition is imposed at every source point, including nonclosed points; it is
local on the source and target. In this condition, standard smoothness at a
prime means that after a further principal shrinking around that prime the
ring map has a standard smooth presentation.

1. **Pointwise criterion.** Let $\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$, put
   $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$ and $\kappa=\kappa(\mathfrak p)$. Then $R\to S$
   is standard smooth at $\mathfrak q$ ([[def-ag-standard-smooth-algebra]]) if
   and only if the local ring homomorphism $R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}$
   is flat and the fibre $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ is geometrically regular
   at $\mathfrak q$ ([[def-ag-geometrically-regular-algebra-and-fibre]]).
2. **Global form.** The map $R\to S$ is locally standard smooth if and only if
   $R\to S$ is flat and every fibre $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$,
   $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R$, is geometrically regular.
3. **Field case.** Let $k$ be a field and $A$ a finite-type $k$-algebra. Then $A$
   is geometrically regular over $k$ if and only if the structure map $k\to A$ is
   locally standard smooth; equivalently, if and only if $A$ admits a standard
   smooth presentation over $k$ at every prime. In that case the relative
   dimension of a standard smooth chart at a prime $\mathfrak q$ is the dimension
   of the regular local ring $A_{\mathfrak q}$ when $\mathfrak q$ is a
   $k$-rational point.

Now let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings with $S$ finitely
presented as an $R$-algebra ([[def-finitely-presented-module-and-algebra]]), let
$\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S$ and let $\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R$.
The **fibre** of $R\to S$ over $\mathfrak p$ is
$S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, a $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$-algebra, and it is
**geometrically regular at $\mathfrak q$** when for every field extension
$K/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and every prime $\mathfrak Q$ of
$(S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p))\otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}K$ lying over the
image of $\mathfrak q$ in $S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, the local ring
$$\bigl((S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p))\otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak p)}K\bigr)_{\mathfrak Q}$$
is regular. A fibre is **geometrically regular** when it is geometrically
regular at each of its points, and the condition is imposed on every field
extension $K/\kappa(\mathfrak p)$, not only on the finitely generated ones; an
empty fibre satisfies the pointwise condition vacuously, and the affine line
over the residue field is the model case.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring. A **standard smooth presentation** of an
$R$-algebra $S$ consists of integers $n\ge c\ge0$, elements
$f_1,\dots,f_c$ of the polynomial ring $P=R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]) and an element $g\in P$
such that
$$S\cong\bigl(R[x_1,\dots,x_n]/(f_1,\dots,f_c)\bigr)_g$$
as $R$-algebras, and such that the Jacobian matrix of
([[lem-ag-polynomial-quotient-differentials]])
$$\Bigl(\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial x_i}\Bigr)_{\substack{1\le j\le c\\1\le i\le n}}$$
has a $c\times c$ minor whose image in $S$ is a unit, that is, an invertible
element. The integer $n-c\ge0$ is the **relative dimension** of the
presentation. The case $c=0$ is allowed and is exactly a localisation of a
polynomial ring, $S\cong(R[x_1,\dots,x_n])_g$; the case $n=c=0$ presents
$S=R[\,]_g$ for $g\in R$, that is a localisation of $R$ itself.

**Finitely presented algebras.** A commutative $R$-algebra $A$ is **finitely
presented** when there are $n\in\mathbb N$ and a finitely generated ideal
$\mathfrak a\subseteq R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$
([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) with $A\cong R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$
as an $R$-algebra.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of
$k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put
$$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$
Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let
$f_1,\ldots,f_r$ be any finite generating list of the actual ideal $I$.
Then the coordinate-velocity map gives a canonical $k$-linear isomorphism
$$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$
The kernel is independent of the chosen finite generating list of $I$. No
reducedness, perfectness, or characteristic hypothesis is needed. Finiteness of
the list is available for every finite $n$ by the finite-variable polynomial
Noetherian result cited below.

Let $X$ be a locally Noetherian scheme and $x\in X$. Write
$R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$, let $\mathfrak m_x$ be its maximal ideal, and set
$\kappa(x)=R/\mathfrak m_x$. The point $x$ is **regular** when $R$ is a
regular local ring, with regularity defined by
$\operatorname{edim}R=\dim R$. Then the intrinsic tangent space $T_xX$ is
finite-dimensional over $\kappa(x)$, and
$$x\text{ is regular}\Longleftrightarrow\dim_{\kappa(x)}T_xX=\dim\mathcal O_{X,x}.$$
This is absolute regularity of the local ring; it asserts no smoothness over a
base field.

A scheme is **locally Noetherian** if it has an affine open cover by spectra of
Noetherian rings. It is **Noetherian** if it is locally Noetherian and
quasi-compact; equivalently, it has a finite affine open cover by spectra of
Noetherian rings.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(A)$. Then
$$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)+\dim(A/\mathfrak p)=\dim A. $$

Let $k$ be a field and let $n\ge0$. Then
$$ \dim k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]=n. $$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring, let $x\in R$ be a nonzerodivisor, and let $\mathfrak p$ be a prime ideal minimal over $(x)$. Then $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k$ be a field, let $A$ be a finite-type $k$-domain, and let $\mathfrak m$ be a maximal ideal of $A$. Then
$$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak m)=\dim A. $$

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}(R)$. The **height** of $\mathfrak p$ is the Krull dimension of the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$:
$$ \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak p)=\dim(R_{\mathfrak p}). $$

Let $A\to C$ be a unital ring map. For any set of variables $(t_i)$ and any ideal $I\subseteq A[t_i]$,
$$(A[t_i]/I)\otimes_A C\cong C[t_i]/IC[t_i].$$
Here the extended ideal is generated by the coefficient images of all elements of $I$. For a multiplicative subset $M\subseteq A$,
$$(M^{-1}A)\otimes_A C\cong \overline M^{-1}C.$$
These are ring isomorphisms; no flatness, finite-generation or nonzero-ring hypothesis is required.

Let $k$ be a field and let $r\ge0$ be an integer. Then $k[x_1,\ldots,x_r]$ is a
unique factorisation domain ([[def-unique-factorisation-domain]]). Every
irreducible element of it is prime
([[def-irreducible-and-prime-elements-in-a-domain]]), and every prime ideal of
height one ([[def-height-of-a-prime-ideal]]) is generated by an irreducible
element.
Let $R$ be an integral domain. A polynomial $f\in R[x]$ is a unit if and only if it is a constant polynomial whose constant value is a unit of $R$.
$R/P$ is an integral domain if and only if $P$ is a prime ideal.

The ring $R$ is **Noetherian** if its regular module ${}_RR$ is Noetherian.
Equivalently, every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated.

Let $K$ be a field ([[def-field]]). Then the only ideals of $K$ are the zero
ideal $(0)$ and $K$ itself
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]],
[[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]); consequently every ideal of $K$ is
finitely generated, and $K$ is a Noetherian ring
([[def-noetherian-ring]], [[def-noetherian-module]]). No choice principle is used.

Let $R$ be a Noetherian commutative ring. Then the iterated polynomial ring
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ of [[def-multivariate-polynomial-ring-by-iteration]] is
Noetherian for every $n\in\mathbb N$.
Correspondence theorem: ideals of $R/I$ correspond to ideals of $R$ containing $I$.

For a prime ideal $\mathfrak p$ of a commutative ring $R$, there is a canonical field isomorphism
$$ R_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\cong\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak p),\qquad r/s+\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\longmapsto (r+\mathfrak p)/(s+\mathfrak p). $$
This quotient is the residue field of the local ring $R_{\mathfrak p}$.

If $D$ is an integral domain, then $D\setminus\{0\}$ is multiplicative. Its localisation
$$ \operatorname{Frac}(D)=(D\setminus\{0\})^{-1}D $$
is the **field of fractions** of $D$. Thus its elements are fractions $a/b$ with $a,b\in D$ and $b\ne0$, modulo the localisation equivalence relation.
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $U\subseteq\operatorname{Spec}(R)$ be Zariski-open, and let $\mathfrak p\in U$. Then there exists $f\in R$ such that $$ \mathfrak p\in D(f)\subseteq U. $$
When these conditions hold, $Z$ has the unique generic point $\mathfrak a$.

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

derivations.claim: R=k[z], S=k[x,y,z]/(y^2-x^3)=R[x,y]/(y^2-x^3); y^2-x^3 is irreducible in k[x,y,z] (monic degree-2 argument with units of k[z][x] and parity of x-degree) and hence prime in the UFD k[x,y,z], so S is a domain and X is integral; S is also the tensor product k[z] (x)_k k[x,y]/(y^2-x^3), so X is the constant family C (x)_k A^1 with C the cusp.

The evaluation S -> k[z] sending x,y to 0 is surjective with kernel q=(x,y)S; S/q=k[z] is a domain so q is prime; q meets R in (0), so f(q)=eta is the generic point of Y and the image closure contains Y, i.e. f is dominant.

k[z] admits the standard smooth presentation k[z]=(k[z])_1 with n=1, c=0, so Y is smooth over k by F1; k[z]=k[x]/(0) and S=k[x,y,z]/(y^2-x^3) are quotients by finitely generated ideals, so Y and X are finite type (F27) and finitely presented (F5) over k.

For every prime p of R, S (x)_R kappa(p) is isomorphic to kappa(p)[x,y]/(y^2-x^3) by F15; over eta it is the cusp over kappa(eta)=Frac(R)=k(z) (F23, F24) and over a closed point (z-t) the cusp over k.

For any field kappa, B=kappa[x,y]/(y^2-x^3) is a domain (irreducible prime element in the UFD, F16/F18) and Noetherian (kappa[x,y] Noetherian by F20/F21, ideals of the quotient finitely generated by F19/F22); also k[x,y,z] is Noetherian by F20/F21 and S=k[x,y,z]/(y^2-x^3), being a quotient of it, is Noetherian by the same F19/F22 argument.
If U is a nonempty Zariski-open subset of Y then eta in U, since otherwise the closed complement would contain eta and hence all of Y by F26; the section point q maps to eta and so lies in f^{-1}(U).

Shrinking U to a principal open D(g0) containing eta via F25 (so g0 nonzero and phi(g0) not in q), smoothness is local on source and target (F1) and the chart map A=R_{g0} -> B=S_{phi(g0)} has B=A[x,y]/(y^2-x^3) by the two isomorphisms of F15, hence is of finite presentation by F5 and standard smooth at q_B by F1 and F4.

For the cusp B over any field kappa: dim kappa[x,y]=2 (F11), (f) is minimal over the nonzerodivisor f so ht((f))=1 (F12), and ht((f))+dim B=2 (F10) gives dim B=1; the maximal ideal m=(x,y)B has ht(m)=dim B=1 (F13) and dim B_m=1 (F14).

At the k-rational point a=(x,y,z) of X, dim S=2 via F10-F14 applied to k[x,y,z] (Noetherian by step 2.1) and dim O_{X,a}=2, while the Jacobian (-3x^2,2y,0) vanishes at a so dim_k T_aX=3 by F7; F8 with local Noetherianness (F9, step 2.1) makes a nonregular. If X -> Spec k were smooth, then F1 would give standard smoothness at a, and since k -> S is finitely presented by step 1.3, clause 1 of F2 would make S (x)_k k=S geometrically regular at a, hence S_a regular by F3, contradicting 3 != 2.

p_A = q_B ∩ A is (0) because q ∩ R=(0) by step 1.2; with B=A[x,y]/(y^2-x^3) from step 2.3, the fibre B (x)_A kappa(p_A) is kappa(p_A)[x,y]/(y^2-x^3) by F15 over A, and kappa(p_A)=Frac(A)=Frac(R)=k(z) by F23 and F24.

For the cusp B over a field kappa the point m is kappa-rational, the Jacobian of y^2-x^3 vanishes at the origin, so T_m Spec B = ker(0: kappa^2 -> kappa) has dimension 2 (F7); since dim O = 1 by step 3.1 and Spec B is locally Noetherian (step 2.1, F9), F8 shows m is not regular.

No nonempty Zariski-open U in Y has f^{-1}(U) -> U smooth; the refuted claim's hypotheses are met (k algebraically closed of characteristic 0, X integral and finite type, Y smooth, f dominant) except the missing smooth-source hypothesis, and X itself is not smooth at the origin, so target-open generic smoothness genuinely needs a smooth source.

boundaries.evidence: The refuted claim quantifies over nonempty target opens; steps 2.2 and 6.1 show that no nonempty open U works, because eta lies in every nonempty open and the fibre at the corresponding point is the nonregular cusp. $r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

For $S\subseteq R$, define $(S)$ to be the intersection of all two-sided ideals
of $R$ containing $S$.  This family is nonempty because it contains $R$, and
[[lem-ideal-criterion-and-intersections]] shows that $(S)$ is an ideal.  For
$a\in R$, the ideal $(\{a\})$ is written $(a)$ and is called **principal**.

If $R$ is an integral domain, then $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is an integral domain for every $n\in\mathbb N$, including $n=0$.

Let $k$ be a field and let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in k^n$. The evaluation map
$$ \operatorname{ev}_a:k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to k,\qquad f\mapsto f(a), $$
has kernel $(x_1-a_1,\ldots,x_n-a_n)$. In particular, this ideal is maximal.

For commutative unital rings $A,B$, the assignment $\varphi\mapsto

$$ \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm CRing}(A,B)\cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm LRS}(\operatorname{Spec}B,\operatorname{Spec}A). $$
Consequently $A\mapsto\operatorname{Spec}A$ is a contravariant equivalence
from commutative rings to affine schemes, with quasi-inverse global sections.

Let $k$ be a field, let $I\subseteq k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ be an ideal with a
specified finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$, and let
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in k^n$ satisfy $f(a)=0$ for every $f\in I$. The
**Jacobian matrix at $a$**, with the equation-row convention, is the $r\times n$ matrix
$$ J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a)=\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t_j}(a)\right)_{1\le i\le r,\,1\le j\le n}. $$
Thus row $i$ is the differential of equation $f_i$, and column $j$ corresponds
to coordinate $t_j$. Formal derivatives are computed on monomials by
$$ \partial_{t_j}(t_1^{e_1}\cdots t_n^{e_n})=\begin{cases}e_jt_1^{e_1}\cdots t_j^{e_j-1}\cdots t_n^{e_n},&e_j>0,\\0,&e_j=0.\end{cases} $$
with the integer coefficient read in $k$, and are extended $k$-linearly. The
definition uses the actual scheme ideal $I$; it does not assume that $I$ is
radical or that $k$ is perfect. For a reduced classical algebraic set over an
algebraically closed field, this specializes to its coordinate ring
$k[X]=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I(X)$ ([[def-coordinate-ring-affine-algebraic-set]]).

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\geq0$ be finite, let $I$ be an ideal of
$k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and put
$$X=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I).$$
Let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in X(k)$, and let

$$T_aX\cong\ker\!\left(J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a):k^n\longrightarrow k^r\right).$$

Let $X$ be a scheme and $x\in X$. Write $A=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ and let
$\mathfrak m_x$ be the maximal ideal of this local ring. The **intrinsic
Zariski cotangent space** of $X$ at $x$ is
$$ C_xX:=\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2. $$
It is a vector space over the residue field
$\kappa(x)=\mathcal O_{X,x}/\mathfrak m_x$
([[def-residue-field-scheme-point]]).

Let $X$ be a scheme and $x\in X$. Write $C_xX=\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2$
for the intrinsic cotangent space from
[[def-zariski-cotangent-space-point]]. The **intrinsic Zariski tangent space**
of $X$ at $x$ is its linear dual over the residue field:
$$T_xX:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\kappa(x)}(C_xX,\kappa(x)).$$
If $\mathfrak m_x=0$, then $C_xX=0$ and $T_xX=0$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathfrak p\subset R$ be a prime ideal. Since $1\notin\mathfrak p$ and the product of two elements outside $\mathfrak p$ remains outside $\mathfrak p$, the complement $R\setminus\mathfrak p$ is multiplicative. The **localisation of $R$ at $\mathfrak p$** is
$$ R_{\mathfrak p}=(R\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}R. $$
Its elements are fractions $r/s$ with $s\notin\mathfrak p$.

On $R\times S$, define
$$ (r,s)\sim(r',s')\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u(rs'-r's)=0\text{ for some }u\in S. $$
The **localisation** of $R$ at $S$, denoted $S^{-1}R$, is the set of equivalence classes for this relation. The class of $(r,s)$ is written $r/s$, and its arithmetic is
$$ \frac r s+\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rs'+r's}{ss'},\qquad \frac r s\frac{r'}{s'}=\frac{rr'}{ss'}. $$
The **localisation map** is the ring homomorphism
$$ \lambda_S:R\longrightarrow S^{-1}R,\qquad r\longmapsto r/1. $$
Every $s\in S$ maps to a unit, with $(s/1)^{-1}=1/s$. The construction permits $0\in S$; in that case the localisation is the zero ring.

Let $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $R$, let $S\subseteq R$ be multiplicative, and let $\bar S$ be the image of $S$ in $R/I$. There is a canonical isomorphism
$$ (S^{-1}R)/(S^{-1}I)\cong \bar S^{-1}(R/I),\qquad r/s+S^{-1}I\longmapsto (r+I)/(s+I). $$
This includes the case $S\cap I\ne\varnothing$, when both sides are the zero ring.

For $\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A$, there is a canonical isomorphism
$\mathcal O_{\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathfrak p}\cong A_{\mathfrak p}$.

base field.

The characteristic of a field is either $0$ or a prime number.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $I\trianglelefteq R$ be an ideal. The **radical** of $I$ is
$$ \sqrt{I}=\{x\in R:x^n\in I\text{ for some integer }n\ge 1\}. $$

**Finite type.** $A$ is **of finite type over $R$**, equivalently a **finitely
generated $R$-algebra**, when $A=R[a_1,\ldots,a_n]$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and
some $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic as an $R$-algebra to
a quotient $R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\mathfrak a$ for some $n\in\mathbb N$ and some
ideal $\mathfrak a$: the map $\operatorname{ev}$ above is then surjective, and
[[thm-first-isomorphism-theorem-rings]] identifies $A$ with
$R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/\ker\operatorname{ev}$; conversely the composite of the
canonical projection with the inclusion of the indeterminates exhibits any such
quotient as generated by the residues of $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

Being locally of finite type is affine-local on both source and target. A
quasi-compact morphism locally of finite type is of finite type; equivalently,
over each affine target open it may be tested on a finite affine source cover.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $k$ be a field and
$X$ a finite-type $k$-scheme. Smoothness of $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is
defined by local standard smooth presentations in

characterization: $X\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is smooth if and only if, for
every field extension $K/k$, every local ring of the scheme-theoretic base
change $X_K$ is regular. Here $X_K$ is formed by tensoring affine coordinate
rings with $K$ and gluing as in
[[thm-ag-field-extension-of-schemes]]. We call this condition geometric
regularity of $X$ over $k$. It retains nilpotents in every field change.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Let $k$ be any field, let $n\in\mathbb N$, put $P=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]$, and
let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in k^n$. Suppose $0\ne f\in P$ and $f(a)=0$. Write
the unique finite homogeneous decomposition
$$
f(a_1+t_1,\ldots,a_n+t_n)=\sum_{j\ge0}f_j(t_1,\ldots,t_n),
$$
where $f_j$ is homogeneous of total degree $j$. The **multiplicity of the
hypersurface equation $f$ at $a$**, denoted $\operatorname{mult}_a(f)$, is
the least $j$ for which $f_j\ne0$.

Let $k$ be any field, $n\in\mathbb N$, $P=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$, and
$\mathfrak q=(t_1,\ldots,t_n)$. Let $I\subseteq\mathfrak q$,
$A=P/I$, $X=\operatorname{Spec}A$, and let $x$ be the rational origin, so
$\mathfrak m=\mathfrak q/I$ and $A/\mathfrak m=k$. For a nonzero polynomial
$f=\sum_d f_d$ decomposed into total-degree homogeneous parts, let $f_{\min}$
be its lowest nonzero homogeneous part, and let
$\operatorname{in}_{\mathfrak q}(I)$ be the ideal generated by all
$f_{\min}$ with $0\ne f\in I$. The canonical graded $k$-algebra map
$$P/\operatorname{in}_{\mathfrak q}(I)\longrightarrow\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m_x}\mathcal O_{X,x}$$
sending each variable to its degree-one initial class, is an isomorphism.
Consequently
$$\operatorname{Cone}_x(X)\cong\operatorname{Spec}\bigl(P/\operatorname{in}_{\mathfrak q}(I)\bigr).$$
If $I=(f)$ with $f\ne0$, then
$\operatorname{in}_{\mathfrak q}(I)=(f_{\min})$. The initial forms of a
chosen generating set for $I$ need not generate
$\operatorname{in}_{\mathfrak q}(I)$.

The **scheme-theoretic tangent cone** of $X$ at $x$ is the affine
$\kappa(x)$-scheme
$$
\operatorname{Cone}_x(X):=\operatorname{Spec}\!\left(\operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m_x}(A)\right)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x).
$$
We use $\operatorname{Cone}_x(X)$ to distinguish this scheme from the
cotangent space denoted $C_xX$ in the preceding definition. Here `Spec` carries its affine scheme structure
([[def-affine-scheme-spectrum]], [[def-affine-scheme]]), and the map to
$\operatorname{Spec}\kappa(x)$ is the structure morphism of a scheme over
$\kappa(x)$ ([[def-scheme-over-base]]) induced by the degree-zero inclusion. The
grading is retained as part of the cone presentation. The reduction
$(\operatorname{Cone}_x(X))_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a closed subscheme that can
differ from $\operatorname{Cone}_x(X)$;
the definition uses the full associated graded ring, without quotienting by
its nilpotents ([[def-reduction-of-scheme]]).

Let $k$ be a field, let $I\subseteq k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]$ be an ideal with a
specified finite generating list $f_1,\ldots,f_r$, and let
$a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in k^n$ satisfy $f(a)=0$ for every $f\in I$. The
**Jacobian matrix at $a$**, with the equation-row convention, is the $r\times n$ matrix
$$ J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a)=\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t_j}(a)\right)_{1\le i\le r,\,1\le j\le n}. $$
Thus row $i$ is the differential of equation $f_i$, and column $j$ corresponds
to coordinate $t_j$. Formal derivatives are computed on monomials by
$$ \partial_{t_j}(t_1^{e_1}\cdots t_n^{e_n})=\begin{cases}e_jt_1^{e_1}\cdots t_j^{e_j-1}\cdots t_n^{e_n},&e_j>0,\\0,&e_j=0.\end{cases} $$
with the integer coefficient read in $k$, and are extended $k$-linearly. The
definition uses the actual scheme ideal $I$; it does not assume that $I$ is
radical or that $k$ is perfect. For a reduced classical algebraic set over an
algebraically closed field, this specializes to its coordinate ring
$k[X]=k[t_1,\ldots,t_n]/I(X)$ ([[def-coordinate-ring-affine-algebraic-set]]).

Evaluation at the origin has maximal kernel (x,y) and kills f, so it factors through A=k[x,y]/(f) as a k-algebra homomorphism A->k, exhibiting the origin as a k-rational point of C.

Since I=(f) is principal with f in the maximal ideal (x,y), the initial ideal is (f_min)=(y^2-x^2) and the scheme-theoretic tangent cone at the origin is Spec(k[x,y]/(y^2-x^2)), with the full associated graded ring and no reduction performed.
The Jacobian matrix of the single generator f at the origin is the zero 1x2 matrix (-3x^2-2x,2y) evaluated at (0,0), whose kernel is all of k^2, so T_0C is canonically k^2.

In k[x,y], (y-x)(y+x)=y^2-x^2, and the two linear factors are non-proportional: proportionality would give 1=c and -1=c, hence 1+1=0 in k with 1 nonzero, contradicting char k != 2. So the cone presents the two distinct lines y=x and y=-x through the origin, each factor occurring once in the degree-two leading form.

Conclusion: at the origin of the nodal cubic the multiplicity of the equation is 2, the tangent space is k^2, the scheme-theoretic tangent cone is Spec(k[x,y]/(y^2-x^2)), the two distinct lines y=x and y=-x, so the singularity has two distinct tangent directions and the leading form is neither a power of one line nor an irreducible quadratic.

Boundary and scope dispositions: nonemptiness of C and of the cone, the zero Jacobian row, the vanishing constant, linear and mixed terms, the single equation, row, cone equation and factor occurrences, the excluded characteristic-2 collapse of the two factors into one doubled line, the degree endpoints 2 and 3, the absence of any choice principle, and the vacuity of the iff axes.

**Jacobian matrix at $a$**, with the equation-row convention, is the $r\times n$ matrix
$$ J_{(f_1,\ldots,f_r)}(a)=\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial t_j}(a)\right)_{1\le i\le r,\,1\le j\le n}. $$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

1. $U$ is finite-dimensional over $F$ and $\dim_F U \le n$;
2. $\dim_F U = n$ **if and only if** $U = V$;
3. **Extension, with no choice principle.** Every linearly independent
   $A_0 \subseteq U$ is contained in a basis of $U$: there is a basis $B$ of $U$
   with $A_0 \subseteq B \subseteq U$. Claim 1 is the case $A_0 = \varnothing$.
   Since $V$ is itself a linear subspace of $V$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]), claim 3
   applies with $V$ in place of $U$, and hence to **any** finite-dimensional
   vector space over $F$ in place of the pair $(V, U)$.

$(p_X\circ\gamma,p_Y\circ\gamma)$ is a $k$-linear isomorphism. No finite-type,
reducedness, or smoothness hypothesis is needed.

Let $A\to B$ and $A\to C$ be maps of commutative unital rings, allowing the zero ring. In the category of all schemes,
$$\operatorname{Spec}B\times_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\operatorname{Spec}C\cong\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A C).$$
The projections correspond to $b\mapsto b\otimes1$ and $c\mapsto1\otimes c$.
$$(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$$
Let $A,B,C$ be commutative $R$-algebras. For every pair of $R$-algebra homomorphisms $f:A\to C$ and $g:B\to C$, there is a unique $R$-algebra homomorphism

Let $R,S$ be commutative rings, let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a ring homomorphism,
and let $(s_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $S$. There is a unique ring homomorphism
A ring homomorphism whose kernel contains a two-sided ideal factors uniquely through the quotient ring.

Let $k$ be a field and let $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in k^n$. The evaluation map
$$ \operatorname{ev}_a:k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\to k,\qquad f\mapsto f(a), $$
has kernel $(x_1-a_1,\ldots,x_n-a_n)$. In particular, this ideal is maximal.

For commutative unital rings $A,B$, the assignment $\varphi\mapsto
\operatorname{Spec}(\varphi)$ gives a natural bijection
$$ \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm CRing}(A,B)\cong \operatorname{Hom}_{\rm LRS}(\operatorname{Spec}B,\operatorname{Spec}A). $$
Consequently $A\mapsto\operatorname{Spec}A$ is a contravariant equivalence
from commutative rings to affine schemes, with quasi-inverse global sections.

Let $X$ be a scheme and $x\in X$. Write $C_xX=\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2$
for the intrinsic cotangent space from
[[def-zariski-cotangent-space-point]]. The **intrinsic Zariski tangent space**
of $X$ at $x$ is its linear dual over the residue field:
$$T_xX:=\operatorname{Hom}_{\kappa(x)}(C_xX,\kappa(x)).$$
If $\mathfrak m_x=0$, then $C_xX=0$ and $T_xX=0$.

derivations.claim: Setup: k[x,y], k[u,v] and k[x,y,u,v]=k[x][y][u][v] are commutative rings; f and g are nonzero; I_1=(f), I_2=(g) are principal and J=(f,g) is generated by the two-element set; A_1, A_2, B, C_1, C_2 and X are formed; f(0)=g(0)=0; T_x denotes the intrinsic tangent space.

Evaluation at the origin has maximal kernel (x,y,u,v), contains f and g, and factors uniquely through B as delta, so the origin is a k-rational point of X; the same argument gives k-rational points 0_1 of C_1 and 0_2 of C_2.

The maps alpha:A_1->B and beta:A_2->B are well defined, induce a unique k-algebra map phi:A_1 tensor_k A_2->B, and the assignment psi on k[x,y,u,v] kills f and g and hence factors through B, giving psi-bar:B->A_1 tensor_k A_2 with the displayed values on the four classes.

The ideal J is presented by the list (f,g), the Jacobian matrix at the origin is the block matrix with rows (0,1,0,0) and (0,0,0,1), its kernel is the two-dimensional space {(a,0,b,0)}, and the Jacobian-kernel theorem gives T_0X isomorphic to that kernel.
For each factor the Jacobian at its origin is (0,1), with one-dimensional kernel {(a,0)} or {(b,0)}, so T_{0_1}C_1 and T_{0_2}C_2 are one-dimensional.

psi-bar and phi are mutually inverse (uniqueness of the coproduct map and of factorization through the quotient), so A_1 tensor_k A_2 is isomorphic to B and the affine fibre product theorem identifies C_1 times_k C_2 with X, carrying the origin to (0_1,0_2).

The product tangent isomorphism of the product lemma, applied to the k-rational points 0_1 and 0_2, gives T_{(0_1,0_2)}(C_1 times_k C_2) = T_{0_1}C_1 direct-sum T_{0_2}C_2 = k^2; under the coordinate-velocity identifications the velocity (a,0,b,0) projects to (a,0) and (b,0), so the direct-sum description and the Jacobian kernel agree.

Conclusion: T_0X is the kernel {(a,0,b,0)} of the block Jacobian matrix, two-dimensional, and the direct-sum formula for the product reproduces the same dimension from the one-dimensional factors, with no characteristic or extra hypothesis.

Boundary and scope dispositions: nonemptiness of X, C_1, C_2, k and the generating lists; the zero cases at the origin and the nonvanishing unit entries; one point, one product isomorphism, one matrix, one kernel description and one dimension per factor; the absence of degenerate zero tangent factors and of any characteristic-specific behaviour; the dimension endpoints one and two; both directions of the kernel characterization and the two-sided inverse of the algebra isomorphisms; and no use of any choice principle.

boundaries.evidence: X, C_1 and C_2 are nonempty because step 2.1 exhibits the origins as k-rational points, and k is nonempty as a field with 0 different from 1; the generating lists of I_1, I_2 and J are nonempty, presented by the single elements f, g and the pair (f,g) in steps 1.1 and 2.3, so no object or list in the statement is empty.

The zero cases are the origin 0 with all four coordinates zero, the vanishing f(0)=g(0)=0 recorded in step 1.1, the vanishing entries -2x and -2u at the origin, the zero vector in the kernel, and the constant based dual-number point; the kernel of step 2.3 is not the zero space but the two-dimensional space {(a,0,b,0)} because the entries 1 never vanish.

There is one origin 0, one product isomorphism, one Jacobian matrix with two rows, one kernel description, two equations, and one dimension contributed by each of the two factors (steps 2.3, 2.4 and 3.1); the direct-sum formula has exactly two summands, and T_0X has dimension two rather than one.

No zero tangent factor occurs, both factors being one-dimensional by step 2.4; no equation degenerates to the zero polynomial since f and g have y- and v-coefficient 1 in step 1.1; and the characteristic does not enter, every evaluated entry of the two Jacobian matrices being 0 or 1 (steps 2.3 and 2.4), so the characteristic-two case is not exceptional.

The dimension endpoints are one for each factor and two for the product (steps 2.3, 2.4 and 4.1); the extreme parameter value a=b=0 gives the zero vector, and the evaluated entries -2x and -2u take the endpoint value 0 at the origin (step 2.3), so no nonzero entry is lost at the endpoint.

No Axiom of Choice or dependent choice is used: f, g, the maps alpha, beta, the assignments defining phi and psi, and the Jacobian evaluations are all exhibited explicitly in steps 2.2 and 2.3, no basis or neighbourhood is selected, and every cited supplier is choice-free with no def-axiom-of-choice dependency declared (step 6.1).

The forward direction of the kernel characterization in step 2.3: if w lies in the kernel of the block matrix then the first row gives w_2=0 and the second row gives w_4=0; also the forward direction of the algebra identification in step 3.1, where the well-definedness of alpha and beta uses y-hat = x-hat squared and v-hat = u-hat squared.

The reverse direction of the kernel characterization in step 2.3: if w_2=0 and w_4=0 then both rows annihilate w, so w lies in the kernel; and the algebra maps of steps 2.2 and 3.1 are two-sided inverses, psi-bar of phi and phi of psi-bar being the respective identities.
